question: An article recently published in the Journal of Phytopathology (‘A decade of monitoring surveys for Xylella fastidiosa subsp. pauca in olive groves in Apulia (Italy) reveals a low incidence of the bacterium in the demarcated areas’)1 analysed a decade of official data and found there to be no correlation between Xylella and the desiccation of olive trees. It also shows: 1.
the very low incidence of olive trees testing positive (including in the infected areas);
the excessive number of healthy monumental olive trees that get uprooted under the ‘50 m radius’ rule, despite the very low incidence of the bacterium;
the epidemiological irrelevance of asymptomatic trees in the spread of Xylella.

On the basis of this data and according to epidemiological models, the study suggests doing away with the obligation to fell all trees within a 50 m radius of the infected plant. In the light of this new scientific evidence: 1.
Does the Commission intend to revise the felling measures in Regulation (EU) 2020/1201?
Will it ask the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization (EPPO) to move Xylella fastidiosa (olive rapid decline complex strain) from the A2 quarantine list to the alert list?

Will it abolish the ban on replanting native varieties, given that a number of scientific publications have confirmed that native olive varieties are more resistant to Xylella than the Leccino olive tree?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.5.2024) The Commission adopted measures against Xylella fastidiosa1 in 2020, following the publication by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) of a risk assessment for this pest2.

The Commission is preparing a new mandate to EFSA to update the risk assessment of Xylella fastidiosa in light of the recent developments of the pest in the EU territory, to ensure the measures take into account the latest technical and scientific knowledge. The Commission will, together with the Member States, revise the current measures if and as appropriate.

The European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organisation (EPPO) A2 list3 includes pests present in the EPPO region and for which it recommends regulating as quarantine pests. The aim of the EPPO alert list is to provide early warning on pests that may pose a risk. This list is also a source of candidates for an EPPO pest risk analysis.

Xylella fastidiosa is already listed in Part B of Annex II to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/20724, as a pest known to be present in the Union territory, and a pest risk assessment from the EFSA exists. According to Regulation (EU) 2020/12015, there is no ban on replanting native varieties more resistant to Xylella fastidiosa than the Leccino olive tree.

Member States are responsible to authorise, in the case of infected zones under containment measures, the planting of plants that are preferably resistant or tolerant to Xylella fastidiosa, with the exception of the last five kilometres of the infected zone closer to the buffer zone.
